mode.name: Myth Buster
mode.description: Names a widespread myth and corrects it.
mode.structure: Myth -> why people believe it -> the reality -> CTA.
mode.avoid: Do not invent the myth; correct it with real, supportable facts only.

hook.instruction: Open by stating a popular myth you are about to break.
hook.exampleForm: "More cleaning product means cleaner. It does not."
hook.forbidGeneric: Do not open with "Let's talk about a common myth."

concept.title: The Ideas Were Never the Problem
concept.core_idea: A myth-buster that names the widespread belief that running out of content ideas is what kills a social strategy — then reveals the real culprit: ideas survive just fine; it's your schedule that murders them. The video follows a product manager at a two-person SaaS team who leaves Monday's brainstorm with a full Notion doc and zero posts by Friday. fenrik Studio is framed as the fix for the execution gap, not the ideation gap.
concept.product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced as the execution layer that exists between 'great idea' and 'actually posted.' It doesn't replace ideation — it makes ideation irrelevant to the production step. The URL is the only input. The content ships. The Notion doc can stay full; it no longer has to become anything.
concept.why_it_works: The myth-buster structure works here because the myth ('we need better ideas') is genuinely widespread and genuinely wrong — which makes the correction feel like an insider reveal rather than a sales pitch. The sticky note visual is immediately recognizable to anyone who has run a Monday brainstorm. The Friday payoff is specific enough to sting without mocking the viewer. The product enters as a systems fix, not a creativity crutch, which respects the audience's intelligence and reframes the value proposition cleanly.
concept.narrative_arc: MYTH: 'We just need better content ideas.' The video opens on a confident statement — a sticky note on a monitor that reads 'CONTENT IDEAS ✅' — implying the hard part is done. BEAT 1 (why believed): People assume the bottleneck is creativity. The brainstorm felt productive. The Notion doc is full. The ideas are genuinely good. Everyone leaves Monday's standup feeling like the problem is solved. BEAT 2 (reality): Cut to Friday. Same desk. Same monitor. The sticky note is still there. The Notion doc is still full — and untouched. Three Slack messages asking 'did anyone post this week?' go unanswered. The ideas didn't disappear. Tuesday had a bug to fix. Wednesday had a demo. Thursday had a board update. The ideas never had a slot. The myth is that you need more ideas. The reality is that ideas without execution infrastructure are just a list. BEAT 3 (resolution): fenrik Studio doesn't ask for ideas. It asks for a URL. Your website already holds everything it needs to build a full content package — videos, captions, posts, hashtags — ready to publish before Friday even arrives. CTA lands clean.
concept.emotional_tone: Wry and conspiratorial — the video treats the viewer as someone smart enough to have already suspected this truth but never said it out loud. No shame, no lecture. The energy is a colleague leaning over and saying 'yeah, we both know what's actually happening here.'
concept.audience_insight: Two-person and small SaaS teams are disproportionately likely to conflate planning with doing. A good brainstorm session produces real psychological relief — it feels like progress. That feeling is exactly what lets the week fill up with everything else. By Friday, the ideas are intact and the feed is empty. This audience knows it happens; they just haven't named the mechanism clearly.

visual_direction.palette: Muted warm neutrals for the desk environment — off-white, light oak, soft grey. Accent color is a single sticky-note yellow that appears in the opening frame and reappears unchanged in the Friday frame, making the visual callback land without narration.
visual_direction.lighting: Neutral daylight through a window on Monday scenes; slightly cooler, dimmer ambient light on Friday scenes — same room, different energy, no dramatic shift. The difference is subtle enough to feel real rather than cinematic.
visual_direction.environment: A compact, shared SaaS team workspace — two monitors, a standing desk partially lowered, a whiteboard in the background with sprint notes. Lived-in but not chaotic. Recognizable to anyone who has worked at or run a small startup.
visual_direction.camera_style: Handheld with minimal movement — slightly documentary, as if someone on the team grabbed their phone to document the week. Quick cuts between Monday and Friday. No transitions, no effects. The edit is the punchline.
visual_direction.art_direction: Flat, functional SaaS workspace aesthetic — the kind of desk that belongs to someone who thinks in sprints. Physical sticky notes coexist with a second monitor showing a Notion doc. The contrast between the tidy brainstorm artifacts and the untouched content queue is the visual story. Text overlays are minimal, dry, and timed to land like a punchline.
visual_direction.character_style: One visible character — a product manager in their late 20s or early 30s, dressed casually (hoodie, no branding). Seen briefly from behind or in partial profile during Monday's brainstorm, then shown at the same desk on Friday, visibly occupied with something unrelated to content. No dialogue required; body language and environment carry the story.

package.title: The Ideas Were Never the Problem
package.hook: You think better ideas will fix your content problem? Think again.
package.scenario: A product manager at a two-person SaaS team runs Monday's brainstorm, fills a Notion doc with genuinely good content ideas, and feels the hard part is done. By Friday, nothing has been posted — Tuesday had a production bug, Wednesday had a customer demo, Thursday had a board update. The ideas are intact. The week is gone.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — Monday, neutral daylight]
HANDHELD SHOT: Desk in a compact SaaS workspace. A sticky note reading 'CONTENT IDEAS ✅' is fixed to the monitor bezel. A Notion doc filled with bullet-pointed ideas is open on the second screen. A product manager (late 20s, hoodie) is seen from behind, nodding.
VO: 'You think better ideas will fix your content problem? Think again.'

[SCENE 2 — Monday brainstorm, tight on Notion doc]
SHOT: Screen-level view of the Notion doc — rows of content ideas, some highlighted, a few tagged with platform names. Looks thorough. Looks done.
VO: 'Monday's brainstorm fills a whole Notion doc. The ideas are good. Everyone leaves feeling like the hard part is done.'

[SCENE 3 — Tuesday through Thursday, quick cuts]
CUT SEQUENCE: Same desk, same room. Tuesday — a terminal window open, someone typing fast. Wednesday — a video call on screen, the product manager mid-sentence. Thursday — a slide deck open, a calendar notification visible. Each cut is fast. No content tools are open.
VO: 'Then Tuesday has a bug. Wednesday has a demo. Thursday has a board update.'

[SCENE 4 — Friday, same desk, cooler ambient light]
HANDHELD SHOT: Same desk. Same monitor. The sticky note — 'CONTENT IDEAS ✅' — is still there, unchanged. The Notion doc is still open, untouched. Three Slack notifications visible on screen. The product manager is leaning back, visibly occupied with something unrelated to content.
VO: 'Friday arrives — same desk, same sticky note, zero posts. The ideas survived. The schedule didn't.'

[SCENE 5 — Closing frame, fenrik Studio logo]
STATIC SHOT: Clean desk surface. The sticky note is the only object in frame. Text overlay appears: 'Your ideas were never the bottleneck.'
VO: 'Your ideas were never the bottleneck.'
LOGO FADE IN: fenrik Studio mark, bottom center.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — Monday, neutral daylight]
HANDHELD SHOT: Desk in a compact SaaS workspace. A sticky note reading 'CONTENT IDEAS ✅' is fixed to the monitor bezel. A Notion doc filled with bullet-pointed ideas is open on the second screen. A product manager (late 20s, hoodie) is seen from behind, nodding.
VO: 'You think better ideas will fix your content problem? Think again.'

[SCENE 2 — Monday brainstorm, tight on Notion doc]
SHOT: Screen-level view of the Notion doc — rows of content ideas, some highlighted, a few tagged with platform names. Looks thorough. Looks done.
VO: 'Monday's brainstorm fills a whole Notion doc. The ideas are good. Everyone leaves feeling like the hard part is done.'

[SCENE 3 — Tuesday through Thursday, quick cuts]
CUT SEQUENCE: Same desk, same room. Tuesday — a terminal window open, someone typing fast. Wednesday — a video call on screen, the product manager mid-sentence. Thursday — a slide deck open, a calendar notification visible. Each cut is fast. No content tools are open.
VO: 'Then Tuesday has a bug. Wednesday has a demo. Thursday has a board update.'

[SCENE 4 — Friday, same desk, cooler ambient light]
HANDHELD SHOT: Same desk. Same monitor. The sticky note — 'CONTENT IDEAS ✅' — is still there, unchanged. The Notion doc is still open, untouched. Three Slack notifications visible on screen. The product manager is leaning back, visibly occupied with something unrelated to content.
VO: 'Friday arrives — same desk, same sticky note, zero posts. The ideas survived. The schedule didn't.'

[SCENE 5 — Closing frame, fenrik Studio logo]
STATIC SHOT: Clean desk surface. The sticky note is the only object in frame. Text overlay appears: 'Your ideas were never the bottleneck.'
VO: 'Your ideas were never the bottleneck.'
LOGO FADE IN: fenrik Studio mark, bottom center.
video.concept: A myth-buster that names the widespread belief that running out of content ideas is what kills a social strategy — then reveals the real culprit: the execution gap. A product manager at a two-person SaaS team leaves Monday's brainstorm with a full Notion doc and zero posts by Friday. The video follows the week, beat by beat, showing how every day consumed the slot that content was supposed to fill. fenrik Studio is introduced as the execution layer — not a creativity tool — that closes the gap between 'great idea' and 'actually posted.'
